concepts.title: Position and displacement
concepts.goals: Choose a signed axis; distinguish position, distance and displacement; calculate a change in position.
concepts.simple: Position locates an object relative to a chosen origin. Displacement compares the finish with the start, without counting the route between them.
concepts.detail: Choose a positive direction before calculating. A coordinate is a location, not a distance travelled. Break a journey into legs to find distance; compare only its endpoints to find displacement. On a line, the sign communicates direction.
concepts.ideas: Distance cannot be negative. Displacement may be positive, negative or zero. A return journey can have a nonzero distance and zero displacement.
concepts.formula: Δx = x_final − x_initial; distance = sum of the absolute lengths of each leg.
concepts.units: Position x and displacement Δx: metres (m). State the positive direction alongside a signed answer.
concepts.example: A delivery robot starts at x = −3 m, visits x = 9 m and stops at x = 4 m. Displacement = 4 − (−3) = +7 m. Distance = |9 − (−3)| + |4 − 9| = 12 + 5 = 17 m.
concepts.real: A batter who runs to the other crease and back covers ground but finishes at the starting position: the net displacement is zero.
concepts.mistakes: Adding every leg gives distance, not displacement. A negative starting coordinate must be subtracted with brackets. Negative displacement does not mean negative distance.
concepts.tip: Write the endpoints first. Check that |displacement| ≤ distance. Equality requires no reversal along the line.
concepts.summary: Choose origin and direction → record endpoints → subtract final minus initial → give metres and direction.
concepts.check: A robot returns to its starting coordinate. Which quantity must be zero?
concepts.why: Its final and initial coordinates match, so their difference is zero. It may still have travelled.

questions.text: A trolley moves from x = −4 m to x = 7 m. Enter its displacement in metres.
questions.solution: 7 − (−4) = +11 m. Subtract the starting coordinate, including its sign.
questions.hint: Identify the relevant quantities and use the formula from this concept. Keep signs consistent.

questions.text: A runner moves 14 m east, then 6 m west. Taking east as positive, enter displacement in metres.
questions.solution: The signed changes add: +14 − 6 = +8 m. The 20 m path length is not displacement.
questions.hint: Identify the relevant quantities and use the formula from this concept. Keep signs consistent.

questions.text: A cart starts at x = 8 m and finishes at x = −5 m. Enter displacement in metres.
questions.solution: Final minus initial is −5 − 8 = −13 m, towards the negative direction.
questions.hint: Identify the relevant quantities and use the formula from this concept. Keep signs consistent.

questions.text: A robot moves from x = 2 m to x = 12 m and then to x = −1 m. Enter total distance in metres.
questions.solution: The two leg lengths are |12 − 2| = 10 m and |−1 − 12| = 13 m. Distance is 23 m.
questions.hint: Identify the relevant quantities and use the formula from this concept. Keep signs consistent.

questions.text: A walker starts at x = −6 m, travels to x = 9 m, then returns to x = −6 m. Enter net displacement in metres.
questions.solution: The endpoints are equal. Net displacement is −6 − (−6) = 0 m, although distance is 30 m.
questions.hint: Identify the relevant quantities and use the formula from this concept. Keep signs consistent.

questions.text: A robot travels only east and west. It covers 38 m total and finishes 10 m east of its start. How many metres did it travel west?
questions.solution: Let E and W be eastward and westward distances. E + W = 38 and E − W = 10. Subtracting gives 2W = 28, so W = 14 m.
questions.hint: Identify the relevant quantities and use the formula from this concept. Keep signs consistent.

concepts.title: Instantaneous velocity and speed
concepts.goals: Relate velocity to the slope of a position–time graph; calculate instantaneous velocity; distinguish speed from signed velocity.
concepts.simple: Velocity describes how position is changing at a particular moment. Speed describes the magnitude of that change without its direction.
concepts.detail: Average velocity compares two times. Instantaneous velocity examines a shrinking interval around one time. On a smooth position–time graph it is the tangent slope. If a formula x(t) is supplied, differentiate it with respect to time.
concepts.ideas: A horizontal tangent means zero instantaneous velocity. A negative slope means motion towards decreasing x. Equal speed does not imply equal velocity.
concepts.formula: v_average = Δx/Δt; v(t) = dx/dt; instantaneous speed = |v(t)|.
concepts.units: Time t: seconds (s); position x: metres (m); velocity and speed: metres per second (m/s).
concepts.example: For x(t) = 2t² − 6t + 1 metres, v(t) = 4t − 6 m/s. At t = 1 s, v = −2 m/s and speed = 2 m/s. At t = 1.5 s the tangent is horizontal.
concepts.real: A game character can run left at 5 m/s or right at 5 m/s. The speed is unchanged but the signed velocity reverses.
concepts.mistakes: Do not use x/t as instantaneous velocity. Do not report a negative speed. Average speed uses total distance, not net displacement.
concepts.tip: Differentiate first, then substitute the requested time. Inspect units of every coefficient.
concepts.summary: Position–time tangent slope gives velocity; take its absolute value to obtain speed.
concepts.check: The position–time tangent slope is −3 m/s. What is the speed?
concepts.why: Speed is the magnitude of velocity, so |−3| = 3 m/s.

questions.text: An object has instantaneous velocity −9 m/s. Enter its speed in m/s.
questions.solution: Speed is |velocity| = |−9| = 9 m/s.
questions.hint: Identify the relevant quantities and use the formula from this concept. Differentiate before substituting time.

questions.text: For x(t) = 5t + 2 metres, enter the instantaneous velocity in m/s.
questions.solution: Differentiating x with respect to t gives the constant velocity 5 m/s.
questions.hint: Identify the relevant quantities and use the formula from this concept. Differentiate before substituting time.

questions.text: For x(t) = 3t² − 2t metres, find velocity at t = 2 s in m/s.
questions.solution: v(t) = 6t − 2. At 2 s this is 12 − 2 = 10 m/s.
questions.hint: Identify the relevant quantities and use the formula from this concept. Differentiate before substituting time.

questions.text: For x(t) = t³ − 6t metres, enter velocity at t = 1 s in m/s.
questions.solution: v(t) = 3t² − 6. At t = 1 s it equals −3 m/s.
questions.hint: Identify the relevant quantities and use the formula from this concept. Differentiate before substituting time.

questions.text: For x(t) = 2t² − 8t metres, at what time in seconds is instantaneous velocity zero?
questions.solution: v = 4t − 8. Solving 4t − 8 = 0 gives t = 2 s.
questions.hint: Identify the relevant quantities and use the formula from this concept. Differentiate before substituting time.

questions.text: For x(t) = t³ − 3t² metres, enter the instantaneous speed at t = 1 s in m/s.
questions.solution: v = 3t² − 6t = −3 m/s at t = 1 s. Speed is the magnitude, 3 m/s.
questions.hint: Identify the relevant quantities and use the formula from this concept. Differentiate before substituting time.

concepts.title: Acceleration
concepts.goals: Calculate average and instantaneous acceleration; distinguish negative acceleration from slowing down.
concepts.simple: Acceleration measures how quickly velocity changes. It can change the speed, the direction, or both.
concepts.detail: On a line, compare signed velocities. Acceleration with the same sign as velocity increases speed; opposite signs decrease speed until any reversal. A velocity–time graph has acceleration as its slope.
concepts.ideas: An object can have zero velocity at one instant and nonzero acceleration. Constant velocity implies zero acceleration; constant acceleration allows velocity to change uniformly.
concepts.units: Acceleration: metres per second squared (m/s²). A value +2 m/s² means velocity increases by 2 m/s each second.
concepts.example: A cart changes velocity from −8 to −2 m/s in 3 s. Average acceleration = [−2 − (−8)]/3 = +2 m/s². It is slowing down because its speed falls from 8 to 2 m/s.
concepts.real: A lift accelerating upwards while descending can reduce its downward speed. The direction of motion and acceleration need not match.
concepts.mistakes: Negative acceleration does not always mean slowing down. Use signed velocities and the time interval, not the clock reading.
concepts.tip: For a speed-change question, compare the signs of v and a. At a turning instant, examine times just before and after it.
concepts.summary: Velocity change divided by elapsed time gives average acceleration. Graph slope or differentiation gives instantaneous acceleration.
concepts.check: Velocity is negative and acceleration is positive, before any reversal. What happens to speed?
concepts.why: Acceleration opposes the current velocity, so the magnitude of velocity decreases.

questions.text: Velocity changes from 3 to 15 m/s in 4 s. Enter average acceleration in m/s².
questions.hint: Identify the relevant quantities and use the formula from this concept. Keep signs consistent.

questions.text: A vehicle maintains velocity −7 m/s for 6 s. Enter its acceleration in m/s².
questions.solution: There is no change in velocity, so acceleration is zero.
questions.hint: Identify the relevant quantities and use the formula from this concept. Keep signs consistent.

questions.text: Velocity changes from −10 to −4 m/s in 2 s. Enter average acceleration in m/s².
questions.solution: [−4 − (−10)]/2 = +3 m/s². The vehicle is slowing while moving in the negative direction.
questions.hint: Identify the relevant quantities and use the formula from this concept. Keep signs consistent.

questions.text: For v(t) = 4t² − 3 m/s, enter acceleration at t = 2 s in m/s².
questions.solution: a(t) = dv/dt = 8t. At 2 s, a = 16 m/s².
questions.hint: Identify the relevant quantities and use the formula from this concept. Keep signs consistent.

questions.text: A ball moving at +6 m/s changes to −2 m/s in 4 s. Enter average acceleration in m/s².
questions.solution: The signed velocity change is −2 − 6 = −8 m/s. Dividing by 4 s gives −2 m/s².
questions.hint: Identify the relevant quantities and use the formula from this concept. Keep signs consistent.

questions.text: For x(t) = 2t³ − 5t² + 4t metres, enter acceleration at t = 3 s in m/s².
questions.solution: Differentiate twice: v = 6t² − 10t + 4; a = 12t − 10. At t = 3 s, a = 26 m/s².
questions.hint: Identify the relevant quantities and use the formula from this concept. Keep signs consistent.

concepts.title: Constant-acceleration equations
concepts.topic: Kinematic equations for uniformly accelerated motion
concepts.goals: Choose an equation from known quantities; use signed displacement; check the constant-acceleration assumption.
concepts.simple: When acceleration stays constant, a small set of equations connects the starting velocity, finishing velocity, displacement and elapsed time.
concepts.detail: Let the initial instant be t = 0. Use one consistent positive direction. The area beneath the straight velocity–time line gives signed displacement. These equations cannot be applied as one interval when acceleration changes partway through.
concepts.ideas: The symbol s is displacement, not always total distance. Free-fall problems use a signed gravitational acceleration. More than one time can correspond to the same position.
concepts.formula: v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²; v² = u² + 2as; s = ½(u + v)t. All require constant a.
concepts.units: u, v: m/s; a: m/s²; s: m; t: s. Convert km/h to m/s before substitution.
concepts.example: A cart starts at 2 m/s and accelerates at 3 m/s² for 4 s. Final velocity = 2 + 3×4 = 14 m/s. Displacement = 2×4 + ½×3×4² = 32 m. The average velocity 8 m/s also gives 32 m in 4 s.
concepts.real: A straight velocity–time segment in a train simulation can be modelled with constant acceleration; a curved segment requires a different approach.
concepts.mistakes: Do not forget the square on time or the factor one-half. Do not use constant-acceleration equations for a variable acceleration. A squared velocity equation cannot by itself determine direction.
concepts.tip: List u, v, a, s and t. Select an equation without the unwanted unknown. Verify physical time is nonnegative.
concepts.summary: Check constant acceleration → choose a positive axis → select an equation → substitute SI units → check the result.
concepts.check: Which condition is required for s = ut + ½at² with a single value of a?
concepts.why: The equation assumes a constant acceleration; u can be nonzero and velocity can change sign.

questions.text: A cart starts from rest with acceleration 2 m/s² for 5 s. Enter its final velocity in m/s.
questions.hint: Identify the relevant quantities and use the formula from this concept. Keep signs consistent.

questions.text: A car moves with constant acceleration from 4 to 10 m/s in 3 s. Enter acceleration in m/s².
questions.hint: Identify the relevant quantities and use the formula from this concept. Keep signs consistent.

questions.text: A cart starts at 3 m/s and accelerates at 2 m/s² for 4 s. Enter displacement in metres.
questions.hint: Identify the relevant quantities and use the formula from this concept. Keep signs consistent.

questions.text: A vehicle moving at 12 m/s brakes at constant acceleration −3 m/s². Enter its stopping distance in metres.
questions.solution: At rest v = 0. From v² = u² + 2as: 0 = 144 − 6s, so s = 24 m.
questions.hint: Identify the relevant quantities and use the formula from this concept. Keep signs consistent.

questions.text: A ball is thrown vertically upward at 20 m/s. Use g = 10 m/s². Enter time to its highest point in seconds.
questions.solution: Up is positive, so a = −10 m/s² and v = 0 at the top. 0 = 20 − 10t gives t = 2 s.
questions.hint: Identify the relevant quantities and use the formula from this concept. Keep signs consistent.

questions.text: A cart starts with velocity +6 m/s and constant acceleration −2 m/s² for 5 s. Enter its TOTAL DISTANCE travelled in metres.
questions.solution: It stops after 3 s, having travelled 6×3 − 3² = 9 m. During the remaining 2 s it travels ½×2×2² = 4 m backwards. Total distance is 13 m, although displacement is 5 m.
questions.hint: Identify the relevant quantities and use the formula from this concept. Keep signs consistent.

concepts.title: Relative velocity on a line
concepts.goals: Express one object’s velocity as observed from another; calculate closing and separation rates.
concepts.simple: Relative velocity answers how fast the separation changes when one moving object is used as the reference.
concepts.detail: First express both velocities on the same axis relative to the ground. Subtract the observer’s velocity from the object’s velocity. Do not blindly add speeds: the algebra already handles opposite directions.
concepts.ideas: Equal velocities produce zero relative velocity. Reversing observer and object changes the sign. A negative relative velocity means motion in the observer’s negative direction.
concepts.formula: v_A/B = v_A − v_B; for constant velocities, relative displacement = initial separation + v_A/B × t.
concepts.units: All velocities must use the same unit, normally m/s. Separations use metres and encounter times use seconds.
concepts.example: A bus moves east at 16 m/s and a cyclist east at 6 m/s. The cyclist sees the bus move east at 16 − 6 = 10 m/s. If they move towards one another at these speeds, the closing speed is 22 m/s.
concepts.real: In a racing game, two cars moving at equal velocity keep the same gap even though both move rapidly relative to the track.
concepts.mistakes: Do not confuse v_A/B with v_B/A. Do not add speeds for objects moving in the same direction. State which object is the observer.
concepts.tip: Draw one axis, attach signs to both ground velocities, then subtract. Check whether the calculated separation grows or shrinks.
concepts.summary: Choose observer B → express both signed ground velocities → compute v_A − v_B → interpret the sign.
concepts.check: Two cars move east with equal velocities. What is one car’s velocity relative to the other?
concepts.why: Subtracting equal velocities gives zero, so their separation stays constant.

questions.text: A moves east at 13 m/s and B east at 5 m/s. Taking east as positive, enter velocity of A relative to B in m/s.
questions.hint: Identify the relevant quantities and use the formula from this concept. Keep signs consistent.

questions.text: Two trains travel east at 11 m/s each. Enter their relative velocity in m/s.
questions.solution: Their equal ground velocities subtract to zero.
questions.hint: Identify the relevant quantities and use the formula from this concept. Keep signs consistent.

questions.text: A moves east at 8 m/s and B west at 4 m/s. Taking east as positive, enter velocity of A relative to B in m/s.
questions.solution: v_A = +8 and v_B = −4. Thus v_A/B = 8 − (−4) = +12 m/s.
questions.hint: Identify the relevant quantities and use the formula from this concept. Keep signs consistent.

questions.text: A cyclist moves at +4 m/s and a bus at +15 m/s. Enter the cyclist’s velocity relative to the bus in m/s.
questions.solution: v_cyclist/bus = 4 − 15 = −11 m/s, backwards relative to the bus.
questions.hint: Identify the relevant quantities and use the formula from this concept. Keep signs consistent.

questions.text: Two carts are 90 m apart and approach each other at constant speeds 7 and 3 m/s. Enter time to meet in seconds.
questions.solution: The closing speed is 7 + 3 = 10 m/s. Time = 90/10 = 9 s.
questions.hint: Identify the relevant quantities and use the formula from this concept. Keep signs consistent.

questions.text: A car is 120 m behind a bus. Both travel east at constant speeds 22 and 14 m/s respectively. Enter the time for the car to catch the bus in seconds.
questions.solution: The gap shrinks at 22 − 14 = 8 m/s. Time = 120/8 = 15 s. Using the sum would incorrectly assume opposite directions.
questions.hint: Identify the relevant quantities and use the formula from this concept. Keep signs consistent.
